name: Aerospace & Defense
one_liner: Designing and building commercial aircraft, engines, defense systems and space hardware, a long-cycle industry defined by huge R&D bets, backlogs and aftermarket profits.
how_it_makes_money: Commercial OEMs sell aircraft to airlines and lessors, often at deep discounts, and engine and component makers earn most profit from decades of aftermarket parts and service. Defense contractors sell to governments under cost-plus or fixed-price contracts, with budgets set by national defense spending. Space companies earn from launches, satellites and government programs.
revenue_formula: Commercial OEM revenue = aircraft deliveries × net price per aircraft
Aftermarket revenue = installed fleet × flight hours × revenue per flight hour
Defense revenue = contract value × % completed (recognized over time)
cost_structure: Materials and purchased components: a large share given long supplier chains
Skilled labor in engineering and assembly
R&D: new aircraft programs cost billions and take years
Program learning curve costs early in production
margins: Defense primes typically earn around high single to low double digit operating margins, with fixed-price programs riskier. Commercial engine and aftermarket players earn strong margins, while new aircraft programs often lose money early. Aftermarket mix, contract type and program maturity drive the spread.

key_metrics.name: Backlog
key_metrics.what: Orders not yet delivered; for OEMs it can span many years of production.

key_metrics.name: Deliveries
key_metrics.what: Aircraft handed to customers, driving revenue and cash.

key_metrics.name: Production rate
key_metrics.what: Aircraft built per month, key for ramping economics.

key_metrics.name: Book-to-bill ratio
key_metrics.what: New orders versus revenue, signaling demand.

key_metrics.name: Aftermarket revenue share
key_metrics.what: Higher share means steadier, higher-margin revenue.

key_metrics.name: Free cash flow
key_metrics.what: Closely watched given heavy working capital and program costs.

trends: Supply chain and quality problems constraining aircraft production ramps
Strong commercial aircraft demand and long order backlogs
Rising defense budgets from geopolitical tension in Europe and Asia
Commercialization of space, with reusable rockets and satellite constellations
Drones, autonomy and software-defined defense attracting new entrants
Sustainable aviation fuel and next-generation engine technology

Should a defense contractor enter the drone market?
Should a supplier acquire a struggling tier-2 parts maker to secure supply?

interview_hooks: Is the Boeing-Airbus duopoly at risk from new entrants like COMAC?
Should defense procurement shift toward new software-driven entrants?
